text: Croagh Patrick stands as a famous site in Irish myth. In Co. Mayo, toward the west, the peak rises from the shoreline to 2,500 feet. Its sharp outline cuts a triangle against the sky. Neolithic ruins rest on its summit, older than the Celtic arrivals. Long ago it bore the name Cruachan Aigle, honouring Aigle. That man died there after hauling rocks up the slopes inside his pockets. Today the mountain carries the name of St. Patrick, who Christianized Ireland. Patrick kept a fast of forty days and forty nights atop it, copying Christ's time in the desert. He then faced the foes of pagan Ireland and overthrew them, embodied by Corra, a demon who sank into a mere at the mountain's foot. The older festivals did not vanish outright; they came back in Christian dress. Lughnasa, a harvest observance of great age, became the rite of climbing the summit on the last Sunday of July. Locals call that climb The Reek. Up to sixty thousand pilgrims make the ascent each year, some going barefoot or on their knees. Princess Grace of Monaco once joined them. To climb hills at Lughnasa was ordinary Celtic custom. The local title Domhnach Chrom Dubh, that is, Crom Dubh's Sunday, points to yet another pagan being that Patrick overthrew.

okr.objective: Croagh Patrick is a sacred 2,500-foot mountain in Co. Mayo bound to St. Patrick and Lughnasa.
key_results: Pre-Celtic ruins on its summit date to the Neolithic period.
Formerly Cruachan Aigle, it now bears the name of St. Patrick, who fasted there 40 days and 40 nights.
Patrick defeated the demon Corra, who drowned in a lake at the peak's base.
Lughnasa was refashioned into the Christian climb known as The Reek on the last Sunday in July.
